title: Famous names of Prairie Avenue
premise: A summer evening on Millionaire's Row: Pullman, Glessner, Kimball, the two Marshall Fields and Armour, and how each one got rich in one lifetime.

opening.text:
JAUNT: FAMOUS NAMES. It is a summer evening on Prairie Avenue in 1904. The lamplighters have lit the street lamps. The carriages are coming home from downtown. Behind these walls live some of the richest families in America. People call this street Millionaire's Row. At one time, sixteen of the city's sixty top business leaders lived here.

There are six houses on foot, from 1729 to 2115 Prairie, going south. First is the man who let people sleep on trains. Next is a man who made farm machines and lived in a stone fort. Then come the piano king, the big store owner and his son. Last is the meat man who used every part of the pig. Each of them got rich in Chicago in one lifetime.

Start at the corner of Eighteenth Street, at the biggest house on the block.

stops.text: This is 1729 Prairie, the Pullman house. Inside there is a theater with about two hundred seats, a pipe organ and a bowling alley. George Pullman got rich young by lifting Chicago out of its mud. He jacked up whole buildings about six feet without breaking them. Then he built railroad sleeping cars. When President Lincoln died, his body rode home in one, and huge crowds lined the tracks. Pullman is dead now, and many of his workers were angry with him. His wife still lives here. The house will be torn down in 1922. Pullman hated one thing on this street. It is right behind you.

This is 1800 Prairie, John Glessner's house. Pullman said he did not know what he had done to have "that thing staring me in the face" every time he went out. Mr. Glessner got rich making farm machines. Two years ago his company joined a giant new one called International Harvester. His architect died just weeks before the building began. The family moved in at the end of 1887 and still lives here. Many years later, people will save this house from being torn down. Across the street, listen for pianos.

This is 1801 Prairie, the Kimball house. It looks like a French castle, with a very steep slate roof and a round tower. William Kimball came to Chicago in 1857 with only four pianos to sell. Later his factory made about a hundred pianos and organs every week. This is his last summer. He will die here on 16 December 1904. Now walk one block south to the richest man in the city.

This is 1905 Prairie, Marshall Field's house. A famous New York architect designed it. Field came from the East. He became the richest and strongest businessman in Chicago. His store's rule was "Give the lady what she wants", and the ladies shopped there and made him rich. He and George Pullman were among the first rich men to buy land here, and the others followed. His house will be torn down in 1955. Next year his world will fall apart, and it starts two doors south.

This is 1919 Prairie, the house of Marshall Field Jr. He bought it in 1890 and kept making it bigger. Two years ago builders added a huge new part. Upstairs live his children, like ten-year-old Marshall Field III. In November 1905 the father will be shot in this house. Two months later the grandfather will die too, after catching a bad cold on a golf course. The boy will grow up in England. For now, the lights are on. One more house is at the end of the walk.

This is 2115 Prairie, the Armour house. The Armour family lived here for almost fifty years. Philip Armour went west during the gold rush. He did not dig for gold. He hired miners to build water ditches. Back in Chicago he built Armour and Company, the biggest food company in the world. He liked to say they used every part of the pig but the squeal. In 1893 he gave a million dollars to start a college. He died in 1901. His wife still lives here. The house will be torn down in 1937.

legs.story: Across Eighteenth Street. The Battle of Fort Dearborn of 1812 was fought in the sand hills under this end of the street.
Across the street to the tower. Kimball's castle faces Glessner's fortress.
South past more big houses. By 1886 the finest houses in the city stood on Prairie Avenue, each with its own carriage house.
Two doors south: father and son lived side by side.
On past Twentieth Street, down the long sidewalk to the last great house.

endings.text:
The walk ends here, at 2115 Prairie. Mrs. Armour stayed. She was one of the last rich people on the street, and she died here in 1927. Most of the others had already gone. A rich lady named Bertha Palmer built a castle by the lake, to the north. Then the other rich families moved north too. One by one, these houses became rooming houses, storehouses and parking lots.

A few houses survived. Glessner's fortress still stands, and so does Kimball's castle. Come back after dark some night, when the street tells its ghost stories.

keepsake.title: Prairie Avenue calling list
keepsake.text: A list of the six houses on the walk. It is a made-up keepsake, not a real calling card from history.

evidence.text: David Kelley-Philip D. Armour Residence. Built 1871. Originally built for lumberman David Kelley, this stately Second Empire residence was for nearly 50 years the home of the family of meatpacker Philip D. Armour.
Philip Armour joined Field and Pullman on the street in 1877.
evidence.locator: The page's history of the street, the paragraph on its first great houses.

evidence.text: Marshall Field Sr. residence at 1905 S. Prairie.

Richard Morris Hunt of New York and Henry Hobson Richardson of Boston were engaged to design the Marshall Field house and another; George Pullman and Marshall Field both acquired property on the street.
evidence.locator: The page's history of the street, the paragraphs on its first great houses and its architects.

evidence.text: Marshall Field Jr. Residence: enlarged and improved several times, the last in 1902, when D. H. Burnham & Company built a huge addition for Marshall Field Jr., who had acquired the property in 1890.
John Glessner Residence. Built 1887; Henry Hobson Richardson, architect. Designed in the Richardsonian Romanesque style, the house is wrapped around a spacious light-filled courtyard.
The family moved into the house in December 1887.
William W. Kimball Residence. Built 1890; Solon S. Beman, architect. Built for the prominent Chicago piano and organ manufacturer in the French Chateauesque style.
J. W. Taylor's photograph of about 1895 shows a very steep slate roof over the main block and a round tower on the 18th Street flank under a slate cone.
evidence.locator: The whole print, from the north-west across 18th Street and Prairie Avenue.

evidence.text: The district marker names George M. Pullman Residence, built 1870-1876, Henry S. Jaffay architect, and (read in paraphrase) a theatre of about 200 seats, a pipe organ and a bowling alley, with later additions by Solon S. Beman including a palm room and a large conservatory.
evidence.locator: The 1729 S. Prairie Avenue entry: its name line, and its description as read in paraphrase.

evidence.text: The route, its order, its dusk, its reading times, its keepsake and its framing are modern interpretation; no historical visit, conversation or occupant on a day in 1904 is asserted.

Mansions for George Pullman, Marshall Field, John J. Glessner and Philip Armour made Prairie Avenue 'Millionaire's Row'; by 1886 'the finest mansions in the city, each equipped with its own carriage house, stood on Prairie Avenue'.

Pullman's firm raised Chicago buildings out of the mud 'on average six feet without causing them any damage'; his first sleeping car 'was finished in 1864'; Lincoln's body went home to Springfield in a sleeper while 'hundreds of thousands of people lined the route in homage'.
evidence.locator: The biography's paragraphs on building-raising, the sleeping car and Lincoln's funeral.

evidence.text: In 1894 Pullman cut his workers' wages, but 'he didn't reduce the rent in Pullman', his company town; he 'died of a heart attack' on 19 October 1897.
evidence.locator: The biography's paragraphs on the strike and his death.

evidence.text: Fearing his body would be dug up, the family had him buried in a 'lead-lined mahogany coffin, which was then sealed inside a block of concrete', under steel rails 'bolted together at right angles', at Graceland Cemetery. An 1897 New York Times account gives a 'lead-lined box wrapped in tar paper' and 'an inch of asphaltum'; behind it, 'a lot of high-profile grave robberies lately' and the fear that 'some of the employees weren't quite done getting revenge'. The historian Adam Selzer: 'Whether it's true or not, we don't really know.'
evidence.locator: The biography's paragraph on the burial; the WTTW piece on the grave.

evidence.text: The 1904 Blue Book lists Mrs. George M. Pullman at 1729 Prairie.
evidence.locator: The street-and-number list, PRAIRIE AV., printed pp. 186-187 (PDF pp. 188-189), as data/residents_1904/households/hh_pullman_mrs_george_m.json reads it.

evidence.text: George Pullman, across the street, complained of the Glessner house: 'I do not know what I have ever done to have that thing staring me in the face every time I go out of my door'.

Kimball founded his piano business in Chicago in 1857, 'beginning with only four pianos'; in 1881 he opened his own factory 'churning out around 100 pianos and organs every week'; he 'died at his home in Chicago on December 16, 1904'.
evidence.locator: The biography: Chicago, the factory, his death.

evidence.text: Marshall Field: 'Give the lady what she wants'; 'the wealthiest and most powerful businessman in Chicago', his fortune valued at $125 million in 1905. His son Marshall Field Jr. was shot on 22 November 1905; Field himself died of pneumonia on 16 January 1906, caught after a New Year's Day golf game with, among others, Robert Todd Lincoln.
evidence.locator: The biography's paragraphs on the store, his wealth, his son and his death.

evidence.text: The Battle of Fort Dearborn occurred in the area that is now the northern section of the street.
At one point in the 1880s 'sixteen of the 60 members of the Commercial Club of Chicago lived on Prairie Avenue'.

Glessner was a partner in Warder, Bushnell & Glessner, farm machinery, of Springfield, Ohio; in 1902 the firm merged with four others to form International Harvester, and he became its vice president. In the 1960s 'the house was threatened with demolition', and it was bought in 1966 'for just $35,000'.

In the California gold rush Armour 'started a business employing out-of-work miners to construct sluices'; Armour & Co. 'became the world's largest food processing and chemical manufacturing enterprise'; he made use of 'everything but the squeal'; in 1893 he gave $1 million to found the Armour Institute of Technology, now the Illinois Institute of Technology; he died of pneumonia on 6 January 1901.
The 1904 Blue Book prints Mrs. Philip D. Armour at 2115; the district marker says Armour's widow was among the last residents of the street, dying there in 1927.
evidence.locator: The street-and-number list, PRAIRIE AV.; the marker's 2115 S. Prairie Avenue entry.

evidence.text: The 1904 Blue Book lists Mr. and Mrs. Marshall Field jr. at 1919 Prairie; their son Marshall Field III, ten years old in 1904, was raised mainly in England after his father's death in 1905.
evidence.locator: The street list as hh_field_marshall_jr.json reads it; the Wikipedia biography of Marshall Field III.

evidence.text: HABS dates the building from June 1, 1886 to December 1, 1887; the house museum gives Richardson's death as April 26, 1886.
evidence.locator: HABS data pages pp. 1-2; the museum's Richardson page.

evidence.text: After Bertha Palmer built the Palmer Mansion on Lake Shore Drive 'the elite residents began to move north'.
George M. Pullman Residence, 1729 S. Prairie Avenue: razed 1922.
Marshall Field Residence, 1905 S. Prairie Avenue: later converted to an aeronautical university. Razed 1955.
David Kelley-Philip D. Armour Residence, 2115 S. Prairie Avenue: razed 1937.
